Introduction

The AI-Software Development Lifecycle (AI-SDLC) helps teams use AI across product development while keeping people responsible for judgement, evidence and decisions.

Target audience

This guide is for in-house development squads within EDS. It gives developers a shared reference for using AI to understand problems, explore solutions, build software and check outcomes.

The guide covers AI-assisted development: work supported by AI tools, whether or not the product itself contains AI.

Why AI-SDLC?

Product development has traditionally been organised around limited specialist capacity. Product management, research, design, engineering, testing, security and operations each have their own priorities, tools and pace, so the lifecycle sequences their effort carefully.

Work passes from opportunity to requirements, design, build, test, approval and launch before the team learns from users. Each arrow is a handoff where work can wait, lose context or be reinterpreted. The dashed path shows that evidence from users returns only after most of the effort has been spent.

Agile, DevOps, continuous delivery and design thinking improved this model through smaller batches and faster feedback. Much of the work is still limited by specialist capacity, handoffs and the cost of changing direction.

AI changes that balance. Research, prototyping, testing and parts of implementation can be produced faster and at lower cost, giving people more capacity to frame problems, assess evidence and make decisions. AI-SDLC uses this shift to pursue faster validated learning: testing assumptions early and using the results to solve user problems sooner.

  1. Reduce the hidden cost of coordination

    Much of the elapsed time in product development accumulates between activities rather than within them. A designer waits for clarification, engineering waits for design and security waits for architecture. When specialists engage one after another, their concerns surface after work has already been built on the assumptions they would have challenged.

    Involve product, engineering, security and other relevant specialists early, and keep feedback flowing throughout development.

  2. Learn before the cost of change grows

    The larger cost is often not building something, but changing direction after it is built. If a team tests a hypothesis in two days and finds that users do not value the solution, it has learned cheaply. The same finding after months of design, build and release preparation means far more work to reconsider.

    Test the riskiest assumptions with small experiments before committing substantial effort. Judge an approach by the cost of gaining useful evidence, as well as the cost of building.

  3. Explore more options before choosing

    When each extra option costs scarce specialist time, teams narrow early: ten ideas become one design before anyone has tested them. AI can reduce the effort of researching alternatives, drafting designs, building prototypes and running tests.

    Generate several options, compare them and combine the strongest elements before committing. The aim is not speed for its own sake, but more evidence before decisions that are hard to reverse.

  4. Make rebuilding a practical option

    When creating another implementation takes less effort, replacing an unsuitable one becomes a reasonable choice rather than a failure. Aim to discover the right implementation quickly, instead of trying to get the first one right. Keep a solution because evidence supports it, not because it was expensive to produce.

    Note

    Some decisions remain costly to reverse: core data models, public APIs, regulatory commitments, major architecture choices, vendor dependencies, user migrations and security models. Make these deliberately, with human judgement.

  5. Improve delivery across the whole lifecycle

    Faster individual tasks do not automatically make delivery faster. If the rest of the workflow stays the same, the queue moves to the next constraint.

    Illustrative examples of how faster tasks can move the bottleneck
    Faster taskIf the rest stays the sameLikely result
    Product requests are drafted fasterEngineering capacity is unchangedThe engineering queue grows
    Code is written fasterSecurity review remains manualSecurity review becomes the bottleneck
    Prototypes are quick to buildUser validation still takes monthsEnd-to-end learning barely improves

    Adapt reviews, approvals and feedback loops alongside individual productivity, so that comparing, approving and revising work can keep pace with generation.

  6. Make evaluation a continuous activity

    When generation becomes cheap, evaluation can become a constraint. Producing more options helps only if the team can decide which of them are useful.

    A failed test is evidence to reassess an option, not a reason to select it. Allow time and people to review results alongside the capacity to generate alternatives.

    Evaluate usefulness and quality as work is created, rather than only at final testing. People frame the problem, weigh the evidence and remain accountable for decisions while AI carries out more of the execution.

  7. Measure how quickly uncertainty becomes evidence

    Features delivered, story points, releases and lines of code describe activity; they do not show whether the team has learned anything or created value. As AI makes output easier to generate, these measures become less informative. A better question is: how quickly can the team turn uncertainty into evidence?

    Example: hypothesise that a clearer upload flow lets at least 8 of 10 pilot users submit the right document unaided, with no wrong-recipient uploads. Test on a prototype. If the agreed threshold is met, commit to a bounded implementation; otherwise revise the flow or stop, and record the evidence. This is an illustrative threshold, not a policy.

    The loop runs from hypothesis to experiment, from experiment to evidence and from evidence to a decision, which informs the next hypothesis. Shorten each turn by lowering the cost of experiments, coordination and changing direction, and by responding sooner to user feedback.

An evergreen development guide

This site is an evergreen guide for EDS developers: a reference to return to as the squad’s work progresses, rather than a document read once. It explains AI-SDLC practices so they can be applied in day-to-day development.

The guidance is expected to change as tools develop and squads gain experience. Each practice records its reasons, so the advice can be revisited when the evidence changes.

To begin, pick one assumption in your current work that would be costly to get wrong. Agree what evidence would help the squad decide, then choose a small experiment to obtain it.
